title: Goldman Sachs Adds a March Rate Hike to Its Federal Reserve Forecast
excerpt: Goldman Sachs now expects the Federal Reserve to raise rates by 25 basis points in March, abandoning its call that the hiking cycle would end in December, after October inflation came in hotter than expected for a third straight month, Reuters reported.
body:
• Goldman Sachs now forecasts a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate increase in March, changing its previous call that the hiking cycle would end in December, according to Reuters.
  • The revision followed October inflation data that marked a third consecutive month of upside surprises; markets fully expect a 25-basis-point hike on December 9, per CME FedWatch.
  • Goldman now expects rate cuts to begin in December 2027, three months later than it previously forecast, followed by cuts in March, June and September 2028.
  • For borrowers, Goldman's path means US rates stay higher for longer: a December hike, a likely March hike, and no relief priced into its forecast until late 2027.

Goldman Sachs has added another interest-rate increase to its Federal Reserve forecast, saying on Tuesday that it now expects a 25-basis-point hike in March after hotter-than-expected October inflation data prompted it to abandon its call for an end to the hiking cycle in December, Reuters reported.

Tuesday's inflation data marked a third consecutive month of upside surprises. Markets are fully expecting a 25-basis-point increase at the Fed's December 9 meeting, according to CME FedWatch pricing cited by Reuters.

Why March, Not January

Goldman said a third hike is more likely in March than in January, because it expects inflation to ease through the end of the year before renewed "start-of-the-year" price pressures, amid elevated costs, lift inflation again. By the time of the March meeting, or even the January meeting, the bank expects the energy shock to feel largely over.

"But we suspect that the recent inflation readings will lead most FOMC participants to signal a third hike in the December dot plot."

— David Mericle, chief US economist, Goldman Sachs

Goldman joins Deutsche Bank in expecting a further hike beyond December. Deutsche expects an additional quarter-point increase in January, on top of increases in December and March, according to Reuters.

Cuts Pushed Further Out

The other side of the revision is how long higher rates last. Goldman now expects rate cuts to begin in December 2027, three months later than it previously forecast, followed by additional cuts in March, June and September 2028.

For households and businesses, the forecast is an expectation, not a Fed decision: Goldman is a brokerage projecting the central bank's path, and the December "dot plot" — the FOMC members' own projections, due with the December meeting — will show whether policymakers share that view. Until then, the direction of travel in Wall Street forecasts is consistent: inflation has surprised on the upside three months running, and forecasters are adding hikes at the front of the path and pushing cuts further back.

What to watch next is the December 9 FOMC meeting itself: whether the Fed delivers the fully priced 25-basis-point increase, and whether its dot plot signals the third hike Goldman now expects in March.
